summary: This Wikipedia-style note explains climate change feedbacks: processes that amplify (positive) or dampen (negative) the warming caused by initial forcings. It surveys the main positive feedbacks (water vapor, carbon cycle releases from permafrost, peat, hydrates and forests, cloud and ice-albedo feedbacks) and negative feedbacks (Planck response, ocean uptake, chemical weathering, photosynthesis), concluding that positive feedbacks outweigh negative ones globally. It also covers the energy-imbalance formulation and implications for climate policy.
one_line: Overview of climate change feedbacks, positive and negative, including water vapor, permafrost methane, ice-albedo, and the Planck response.
key_facts: Climate change feedbacks are effects of global warming that amplify or diminish the effect of the forces that initially cause the warming.
Positive feedbacks enhance global warming while negative feedbacks weaken it.
Observations and modeling studies indicate that globally the positive feedbacks outweigh the negative feedbacks, producing a net positive feedback to Earth's global warming.
The IPCC Fourth Assessment Report projected warming between the late 20th and late 21st century of 1.1 to 6.4 °C as the 'likely' range.
Western Siberia is described as the world's largest peat bog, a one million square kilometer region of permafrost peat bog formed 11,000 years ago.
As much as 70,000 million tonnes of methane might be released from thawing Western Siberian permafrost over the next few decades.
Water vapor feedback is strongly positive, with most evidence supporting a magnitude of 1.5 to 2.0 W/m/K, sufficient to roughly double the warming that would otherwise occur.
The Planck feedback is estimated from the derivative of the Stefan–Boltzmann equation as -4σT = -3.8 W/m/K.
The IPCC Third Assessment Report (2001) judged an abrupt release of atmospheric methane to be 'exceptionally unlikely' (less than a 1% chance).
The CCSP assessment published in 2008 concluded that an abrupt release of methane into the atmosphere appeared 'very unlikely' (less than 10% probability).
In 2008, a research expedition for the American Geophysical Union detected methane levels up to 100 times above normal in the Siberian Arctic.
Bellamy et al. (Nature, September 2005) reported UK soils losing carbon at four million tonnes a year for the past 25 years.
The Sixth IPCC Assessment Report states that permafrost thaw will lead to some additional warming but not a 'runaway warming' situation.
Louise M. Farquharson and her team estimated about 600,000 square kilometers of permafrost, about 5.5% of the year-round permafrost zone, is vulnerable to rapid surface thawing.
Most (~75%) of the CO2 emitted by human activities is expected to dissolve in the ocean over a period of centuries.

entities.name: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
entities.role: Produced assessment reports (AR4, Third and Sixth Assessment Reports, 2021 glossary) that project warming and assess feedbacks and methane release.

entities.name: Bellamy et al.
entities.role: Authors of a Nature paper (September 2005) reporting UK soil carbon losses.

entities.name: Chris Freeman
entities.role: Suggested that release of dissolved organic carbon from peat bogs is a positive feedback for global warming.

entities.name: Turetsky et al.
entities.role: Reported in April 2019 that permafrost was thawing quicker than predicted.

entities.name: Louise M. Farquharson
entities.role: Led a 12-year study of Canadian permafrost reported on 10 June 2019.

entities.name: Mark Serreze
entities.role: Of the US National Snow and Ice Data Center; views 2030 as a 'reasonable estimate' for when the summertime Arctic ice cap might be ice-free.

entities.name: Lawrence et al.
entities.role: Suggested in 2008 that rapid melting of Arctic sea ice may start a feedback loop melting Arctic permafrost.

entities.name: American Geophysical Union
entities.role: Sponsored a 2008 research expedition that detected high methane levels in the Siberian Arctic.

entities.name: Climate Change Science Program (CCSP)
entities.role: US program whose 2008 assessment judged an abrupt methane release very unlikely.

entities.name: Western Siberia
entities.role: Described as the world's largest peat bog, with permafrost whose thawing could release large quantities of methane.

entities.name: Permian–Triassic extinction event
entities.role: Mass extinction event that the methane clathrate release theory has been proposed to explain.

entities.name: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
entities.role: Climate change event that the methane clathrate release theory has been proposed to explain.

entities.name: Kyoto Treaty
entities.role: Treaty under which the UK achieved annual carbon dioxide emission reductions of 12.7 million tons of carbon per year.

entities.name: C4MIP study
entities.role: Study of 11 models finding a larger fraction of anthropogenic CO2 stays airborne when climate change is accounted for.

entities.name: HadCM3
entities.role: Climate model indicating a secondary carbon cycle feedback from loss of much of the Amazon Rainforest.
